compression.title: AttributionBench
compression.lede: is a benchmark of automatic attribution evaluation from the OSU NLP Group: seven existing datasets in one format, each claim–evidence pair labelled attributable or not (arXiv:2402.15089; census record). It tests support, which the archive keeps apart from lineage and credit (#716; #725).

sentences.text: AttributionBench is a benchmark that tests one relation of provenance, support: its makers present it as "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets" (arXiv:2402.15089; ACL Anthology), and the provenance census records it as a benchmark of the OSU NLP Group whose capability is to test, its object "a generated claim and the evidence it cites" (provenance census record).

The task is the paper's definition of attribution, "whether every claim within the generated responses is fully supported by its cited evidence," an open problem whose verification has depended on "costly human evaluation," and the benchmark is offered "To bridge the gap in the absence of standardized benchmarks for these methods" (arXiv:2402.15089); the census carries that relation, support, through "citations in a generated answer" (provenance census record).

Its setting is the generative search engine that cites evidence to make LLM responses reliable (arXiv:2402.15089), and the archive names the measurement traditions of this class, RAG faithfulness and citation precision/recall among them, as adjacent to its Provenance Erasure Rate, "related to but distinct from" it (#725).

The unit is a claim, "Part of the response to the question," beside references, "A list of documents or paragraphs which could support the claim," labelled "attributable" or "not attributable" (GitHub README), which the census gives as "a claim–evidence pair with a binary attribution label" (provenance census record).
In that unit the README marks the field for citation links as reserved (GitHub README).

Its makers built it "from multiple existing data sources in a unified format, in order to create a unified and diverse testbed for evaluating advanced attribution evaluation systems," with an in-domain training set and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card; the census's aggregation quote).

The seven sources are ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA and LFQA in distribution and BEGIN, HAGRID and AttrEval-GenSearch out of it, with 13,322 training, 1,198 development and 1,610 test items in distribution and 1,686 test items out, every subset label-balanced "to treat the two classes equally" (project page), in four configurations on the dataset card (dataset card).

The makers ask that the constituent datasets be credited with their own work ("If used, please also cite the original datasets accordingly," project page), and the census leaves those datasets unchecked one by one (provenance census record).

On Hugging Face it is a text-classification dataset in English of 10K–100K items under apache-2.0 (Hugging Face; dataset card; provenance census record), 26.4k rows in its full configuration, with 1,481 downloads in the month before the fetch and models trained on it (Hugging Face).

Its authors are Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University (arXiv:2402.15089; project page): the paper was submitted on 23 February 2024, code and data released on 26 February and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May (project page; GitHub README), and it is published as 2024.findings-acl.886, pages 14919–14935 (ACL Anthology).

The dataset sits under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face), the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 by its model name (GitHub README), and the census records the lifecycle as published, at "arXiv:2402.15089" (provenance census record).

The headline finding is that "even a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 only achieves around 80% macro-F1 under a binary classification formulation," the challenge holding "even for state-of-the-art LLMs" (arXiv:2402.15089), and the census carries it as what the benchmark found to survive (provenance census record).

Zero-shot, models reach around 60–70% on the longer-evidence sets and under about 60% on ExpertQA; fine-tuning on NLI-related data helps, fine-tuning on AttributionBench raises the average by 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and "Simply switching stronger models cannot significantly improve the performance" (project page).
Appending questions and responses to the input "is not the key to solving this task," and prompt engineering "only brings limited gain over 7 test sets" (project page).

Of more than 300 error cases, a majority stem from the model's inability to process nuanced information and from the gap between what the model and the annotators can see (arXiv:2402.15089): over 66% from fine-grained information insensitivity, and about 26.8% from the mismatch of accessible information, which "brings into question the reliability of labels within current attribution evaluation datasets," the types tabled at 66.0%, 15.6% and 11.2% (project page).

The project page states the limits of its evidence and its result: "The references are usually manually extracted from webpages by human annotators based on what they think is useful," and "there is still a large room for improvement" (project page).

The Capture Registry records that the census record carries neither the 66% nor the 27% figure and that they are unchecked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); both stand on the project page (project page).

The archive's account of the class begins from the same distinction the benchmark tests: frameworks of this kind "ask whether generated claims are *supported* by cited sources," while the Provenance Erasure Rate asks "what fraction of source-dependent composition occurs without *any* attributional return," so that existing work "evaluates citation quality where citation is attempted" and PER measures the failure to attempt attribution, "an attrition metric rather than a verification metric" (#716).

#716 tables what support metrics miss, "Whether *all* source-dependent claims are cited," calls PER "complementary to, not competitive with, existing metrics," and reports the generative-search audit in which only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations and 74.5% of citations supported their sentence (#716).

In #725 the line runs between support and lineage: RAG faithfulness "asks whether an answer is *supported by* retrieved sources," semantic provenance whether it "*preserves the lineage*" of the meaning it uses, and "A faithful RAG answer can have high PER if it summarizes accurately while stripping authorial framework membership"; citation precision asks whether cited sources contain the cited claim, PER whether the lineage survived "even if no formal citation is made" (#725).

#725 places attribution scores as "Industrial-grade infrastructure for support" whose semantic-provenance-aware variants "are not yet standard" and records, as a hypothesis for later compositions, that support and lineage be told apart (#725); #95 holds that the infrastructure for attribution evaluation "already exists in the research literature" and "can be extended" (#95).

At this entity the census record states the same line in its own words, "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (provenance census record), which the Capture Registry calls "the line between this entity and the next" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); #1611 lists attribution survival beside "the citation-recall and faithfulness metrics of retrieval-augmented evaluation" as a convergence for which "No priority is claimed" (#1611).

#141 sets attribution and faithfulness metrics, which "measure whether generated statements are supported by and attributed to their sources," beside PER's rate of attribution failure at claim grain, and asks of them a further question it marks unmeasured: "whether the attribution failure is power-conditioned" (#141).

The audits of citation support are read as a starting point: "a convincing sentence and a supporting citation are separate achievements" (#1695), and citation recall and precision are checked "apart from whether the territory and its operations survive" (#1705).

#1695 adds the entity question support leaves open: "Local support must therefore be read alongside the identity of the object to which the answer attaches it. A set of true statements can compose a false identification" (#1695); and #1680 states that "A high attribution score with a distorted identity fails this packet's central test" (#1680).

AttributionBench is a different entity from AttriBench: the census record's tag reads "NOT AttriBench: it asks whether evidence supports a claim, not who wrote a quote," and records the neighbour's context as "quote attribution, author, suppression, Berman et al., 2026" (provenance census record).

The census places it in the lineage of answer engines, records the operation it tests as "generation with citations by search-augmented models," and asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", each field's quote "verbatim from a saved source" (provenance census record).

Wikipedia has no article: the title returns "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name," and a search of article space for the name reports "There were no results matching the query." (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

At its bare name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry records the entity identified "from the paper and its repositories," its task and headline figure the census record's quotes from the project page, checked against the census record and its saved pages, and AttriBench "respected by silence" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It records the benchmark "composed at full grain from its own paper" and "its makers are left in the cards": the four authors named in the arXiv and Hugging Face cards, neither they nor the OSU NLP Group in the answer, and no card citing the record that landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
